title: If You Turned 18 in 1957, This Is What Adulthood Really Looked Like

scenes.text: If you turned eighteen in nineteen fifty-seven, you were born around nineteen thirty-nine. You were a baby when the war began, and a little child when it ended. And on a warm June evening in nineteen fifty-seven, you walked across a stage in a cap and gown, and somebody handed you a rolled-up piece of paper tied with a ribbon.
scenes.caption: JUNE 1957

scenes.text: Your mother cried. Your father shook your hand like you were a man, or kissed your cheek and told you how proud he was. And that night, after the party, you lay awake in the same bedroom you'd slept in your whole life, and you wondered what came next.
scenes.caption: WHAT COMES NEXT?

scenes.text: Here is what most people today don't realize. At eighteen, in nineteen fifty-seven, the country considered you old enough to work full time, old enough to marry, and, if you were a young man, old enough to be called into the army. But in almost every state, you were not old enough to vote. That wouldn't change for another fourteen years.
scenes.caption: OLD ENOUGH TO SERVE, NOT TO VOTE

scenes.text: So what did adulthood really look like, for an eighteen-year-old in nineteen fifty-seven? The jobs, the paychecks, the rent, the cars, the dates and the weddings. And the strange, frightening autumn when the whole country looked up at the sky. Let's go back and find out.
scenes.caption: IF YOU TURNED 18 IN 1957

scenes.text: High school graduation in nineteen fifty-seven meant more than it does today. For a lot of families, you were the first one to finish. Your parents had grown up in the Depression. Many of them had left school at fourteen or fifteen to help put food on the table. So that diploma, in its stiff little cover, went straight onto the mantelpiece.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST TO GRADUATE

scenes.text: There was the yearbook, full of signatures. Never change. Stay sweet. Good luck in everything. There was the class ring you'd paid for in installments. And there was the senior prom a few weeks before, in a gymnasium hung with crepe paper, the girls in full-skirted gowns and the boys in rented white dinner jackets.
scenes.caption: THE SENIOR PROM

scenes.text: The senior class picture was taken on the front steps of the school, everybody squinting into the sun, the tall boys in the back row. Somewhere in a drawer, or in a box in the attic, you probably still have that photograph. And if you look closely, you can still name almost every face in it.
scenes.caption: THE CLASS PICTURE

scenes.text: After the ceremony, some of the kids drove out to the lake, or to somebody's farm, and sat around a fire until the sky got light. You made promises to stay in touch. Some of you did. Most of you didn't. Within a year, that whole class would be scattered across the country, in the army, in offices, in factories, in kitchens of their own.
scenes.caption: SCATTERED IN A YEAR

scenes.text: At the commencement ceremony, the speaker, usually a local minister or the mayor or a proud old principal, told you that you were stepping into the atomic age. A world of jet planes, television, and wonders nobody could imagine yet. He said the future belonged to you. And for once, the grown-ups were not exaggerating.
scenes.caption: THE ATOMIC AGE

scenes.text: For the girls, the questions were different, and often the answers had already been decided for them. A job, for a little while. Maybe secretarial school. Maybe nursing. And then, everyone assumed, marriage. For the boys, there was one question that hung over everything else. What about the draft?
scenes.caption: TWO DIFFERENT FUTURES

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-seven, America had a peacetime draft. Every young man had to register with the Selective Service when he turned eighteen. You walked into the local board office, filled out a card, and they gave you a small paper card of your own, which you were supposed to carry with you at all times.
scenes.caption: REGISTER AT 18

scenes.text: You might not be called right away. Some young men were deferred for college, or for farm work, or for a family that depended on them. But a lot of eighteen and nineteen-year-olds simply chose to enlist, to get it over with, or to pick their branch before somebody picked it for them. The Navy. The Air Force. The Marines.
scenes.caption: ENLIST OR WAIT

scenes.text: There was another option, too. Under a law passed in nineteen fifty-five, a young man could join the reserves, serve around six months of active duty, and then spend the next several years training on weekends and in the summer. For a boy who wanted to start a job or marry his sweetheart, that was often the choice his father recommended.
scenes.caption: THE SIX-MONTH OPTION

scenes.text: Two years of active duty was typical for a draftee. You got on a bus, with a small bag, and your mother standing on the curb. And a few weeks later you had a shaved head, a pair of boots, and a drill sergeant who seemed to know your name before you'd ever said it.
scenes.caption: BASIC TRAINING

scenes.text: And then there were the letters. Every evening at mail call, the sergeant read out the names, and you waited to hear yours. A letter from your mother, with news about the neighbors. A letter from your girl, sometimes perfumed, which you read three or four times and kept in your footlocker. In those years, a letter was the only line home.
scenes.caption: MAIL CALL

scenes.text: Even the most famous young man in America wasn't spared. In December of nineteen fifty-seven, Elvis Presley received his draft notice. He was inducted the following March, and the newspapers photographed the army barber cutting off his famous hair. If the king of rock and roll had to go, everybody understood that you did too.
scenes.caption: DECEMBER 1957: ELVIS IS DRAFTED

scenes.text: For many young men from small towns, the service was the first time they had ever left their state. They saw Germany, or Korea, or Texas, which seemed just as far away. They learned to fix engines, run radios, and get along with men from every corner of the country. And a lot of them came home changed.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST TIME AWAY FROM HOME

scenes.text: Some of the young men of the class of nineteen fifty-seven would make the army their career. Others counted down every single day until their discharge. But almost all of them, years later, would say the same thing. The service taught them how to work, how to follow orders, and how to look after the man next to them.
scenes.caption: WHAT THE SERVICE TAUGHT

scenes.text: If you weren't in uniform, you went to work. And in nineteen fifty-seven, a young person with a high school diploma could find a job. The factories were busy. The new suburbs needed builders, plumbers, and electricians. The offices downtown needed clerks and typists. The phone company needed operators.
scenes.caption: PLENTY OF WORK
scenes.chapter: Your first job and your first paycheck

scenes.text: Maybe you walked into the personnel office at the plant in your best clothes, and filled out a form, and started on Monday. On the line, the work was hard and loud and repetitive, but the union had fought for good wages, and the plant had a pension, and your father might have worked there for twenty years already.
scenes.caption: A JOB AT THE PLANT

scenes.text: You punched a time clock at seven in the morning, carrying a metal lunch pail your mother packed the night before, the same kind your father carried. At noon a whistle blew, and everybody sat on crates and benches and ate together. At three-thirty, the whistle blew again, and the parking lot emptied in five minutes flat.
scenes.caption: THE WHISTLE AT NOON

scenes.text: If you were a young woman, the job might be in an office, in a long room full of desks called the typing pool. You sat in rows with the other girls, typing letters on heavy manual typewriters, with carbon paper between the sheets, under the eye of a supervisor who checked every page for mistakes.
scenes.caption: THE TYPING POOL

scenes.text: Before you got that job, you might have taken typing and shorthand in high school, or spent a few months at a business college downtown. A girl who could type sixty words a minute, take dictation in shorthand, and answer the telephone in a pleasant voice was in demand everywhere. Those skills paid the rent for a great many young women.
scenes.caption: SIXTY WORDS A MINUTE

scenes.text: Or you might be a telephone operator, wearing a headset, sitting in front of a great wall of plugs and cords, connecting calls all day long. Number, please. You said it a thousand times a shift. Or you worked behind the counter at the department store downtown, in a neat dress, with your hair just so.
scenes.caption: NUMBER, PLEASE

scenes.text: The boys who didn't go to the plant found other work. Pumping gas and checking oil at the filling station. Bagging groceries at the new supermarket. Loading trucks at the lumber yard. Working behind the soda fountain at the drugstore, in a white paper hat, making malts for the kids who were still in school.
scenes.caption: THE SODA JERK

scenes.text: The federal minimum wage was one dollar an hour. According to the Social Security Administration, the average American worker earned a little over three thousand, six hundred dollars that year. For an eighteen-year-old starting out, it was less. But you'd never had that much money in your life.
scenes.caption: MINIMUM WAGE: $1.00 AN HOUR

scenes.text: Your first paycheck came on a Friday, sometimes in a small brown envelope with the cash already counted out inside. And in a lot of families, the rule was simple. If you lived at home, you gave some of it to your mother for room and board. The rest was yours. You'd never felt so grown up in your life.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST PAYCHECK

scenes.text: And on a farm, the job was the same one it had always been. Up before dawn, milking, feeding, fixing fences, and the long days of harvest. Many farm kids stayed, and took over from their fathers. Many others left for the cities, because a factory paycheck came every Friday, rain or shine.
scenes.caption: THE FARM KIDS

scenes.text: You also got your Social Security card, if you didn't have one already, and you watched them take a little out of every check. You didn't think much about it at the time. Nearly seventy years later, a lot of you are still glad you didn't.
scenes.caption: YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY CARD

scenes.text: Most eighteen-year-olds in nineteen fifty-seven still lived at home. Moving out usually meant one of two things. You were going into the service. Or you were getting married. Living alone, just for the sake of it, was unusual, and for a young woman, many parents considered it out of the question.
scenes.caption: STILL LIVING AT HOME

scenes.text: But if you did find a place, it might be a rented room in a boarding house, with a landlady who served breakfast at seven and locked the front door at eleven. Or a small apartment above a store, shared with a friend from work, with a hot plate, a sink, and a radiator that banged all night.
scenes.caption: A ROOM OF YOUR OWN

scenes.text: There was no washing machine in most small apartments. On Saturday mornings you carried a bag of laundry to the new coin laundromat down the street, fed quarters into the machines, and sat on a plastic chair reading a magazine. It was one of the small, ordinary rituals of being on your own for the first time.
scenes.caption: THE LAUNDROMAT

scenes.text: Rent was cheap by today's standards. By the census of nineteen sixty, the typical American rent was about seventy dollars a month. Gas cost around thirty cents a gallon. A hamburger at a diner was a quarter or so. A pack of cigarettes was about the same, and almost everybody smoked them.
scenes.caption: RENT ABOUT $70 A MONTH

scenes.text: And yes, almost everybody smoked. In the office, at the dinner table, in the car with the windows up, in the hospital waiting room. Doctors appeared in cigarette advertisements. It would be years before most people understood what it was doing to them.
scenes.caption: EVERYBODY SMOKED

scenes.text: There were no credit cards in most people's wallets. If you wanted something, you saved for it, or you bought it on the installment plan, a few dollars a month, with a little payment book you took to the store. A charge account at the department store was a sign that you'd arrived.
scenes.caption: THE INSTALLMENT PLAN

scenes.text: Your first big purchase might have been a radio, a record player, or a portable television, bought from the appliance store downtown. Maybe it was a good suit, for job interviews and weddings and funerals, the only one you owned for years. You took care of things then, because replacing them was not easy.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST BIG PURCHASE

scenes.text: You opened your first savings account at the bank downtown, and they gave you a little passbook. Every time you made a deposit, the teller stamped it and wrote the new balance in ink. Watching that number grow, a few dollars at a time, was one of the quiet pleasures of being grown.
scenes.caption: THE PASSBOOK

scenes.text: And at the end of the month, you sat down at the kitchen table with a pencil and a little notebook, and you added it all up. Rent. Groceries. Bus fare or gas. Something for the church collection plate. Something for savings, if you could. Your parents had taught you that a dollar was hard to earn, and easy to lose.
scenes.caption: BALANCING THE BOOKS

scenes.text: Now let's talk about love. Because if you turned eighteen in nineteen fifty-seven, there's a good chance you were married within a few years. In the late nineteen fifties, Americans married younger than at almost any other time in the twentieth century.
scenes.caption: MARRIED YOUNG
scenes.chapter: Love, dating and getting married young

scenes.text: According to the Census Bureau, the typical bride in those years was only around twenty years old, and the typical groom was around twenty-two. Today, both are about ten years older. Your parents might have married at that age too. It didn't seem young to anybody. It seemed like the next step.
scenes.caption: BRIDE ~20 · GROOM ~22

scenes.text: Dating had its rules. The boy asked. The boy picked her up at her front door, and met her father, who looked him over very carefully. The boy paid. A date might be a movie, a soda at the drugstore, a dance, or a drive out to the lake. And she was home by the time her father said, not one minute later.
scenes.caption: THE RULES OF DATING

scenes.text: Going steady was serious business. A boy gave a girl his class ring, and she wore it on a chain around her neck, or wrapped it with tape or angora yarn so it would fit her finger. Or he gave her his letterman's jacket. Everyone at school knew what it meant.
scenes.caption: GOING STEADY

scenes.text: Double dates were common, two couples in one car, because only one of the boys had a car worth borrowing. You went to the drive-in, and the boys bought popcorn, and nobody watched very much of the movie. Or you went bowling, which was hugely popular in those years, with new alleys opening all over the country.
scenes.caption: THE DOUBLE DATE

scenes.text: And then, one evening, on a porch, or in a parked car, or at the table in her mother's kitchen, he asked. The engagement ring might have cost him a couple of months' pay. The wedding was in the church you'd both grown up in, followed by cake and punch in the church hall, and a honeymoon at Niagara Falls if you were lucky, or a weekend at a lake cabin if you weren't.
scenes.caption: THE HONEYMOON

scenes.text: Before the wedding, there was a bridal shower, where the women of the family gave the bride everything a new home would need. A toaster. A set of mixing bowls. Towels with her new initials. Many couples received a set of china they would keep for the rest of their lives, and bring out only on Thanksgiving and Christmas.
scenes.caption: THE BRIDAL SHOWER

scenes.text: And very often, the babies came quickly. Nineteen fifty-seven was the peak of the baby boom. According to government records, about four point three million babies were born in America that year, more than in any year before it. If you married young, you were part of that story, whether you planned to be or not.
scenes.caption: 1957: THE PEAK OF THE BABY BOOM

scenes.text: When the baby came, the father did not go into the delivery room. He paced the waiting room down the hall, with other nervous fathers, smoking and checking his watch. When a nurse finally came out and told him it was a boy, or a girl, he handed out cigars to everybody in the room. Many of you were that father.
scenes.caption: THE WAITING ROOM

scenes.text: For many young women, marriage also meant the end of the job. Some companies expected a woman to leave when she married, and almost all expected her to leave when she was expecting. It wasn't always what she wanted. It was simply how things were done. Many of those women went back to work years later, and their daughters would grow up in a very different world.
scenes.caption: HOW THINGS WERE DONE

scenes.text: A young couple with a little money saved, and a veteran's loan if the husband had served, could buy a small house in one of the new subdivisions. Two bedrooms, a little yard, and a mortgage that felt enormous. Many young couples moved in with a card table, two chairs and a mattress, and filled the rest in over the years.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST HOUSE

scenes.text: Whether you were single or married, you needed a car. And in nineteen fifty-seven, American cars were at their most spectacular. Long, low, two-toned, covered in chrome, and growing fins on the back like rocket ships.
scenes.caption: 1957: CHROME AND FINS

scenes.text: The car of the year, for many people then and now, was the nineteen fifty-seven Chevrolet Bel Air. Turquoise and white, or red and white, with those sharp little fins and that gleaming grille. It cost a little over two thousand dollars new, which was far more than an eighteen-year-old could afford. But you could dream.
scenes.caption: THE '57 CHEVY

scenes.text: Ford had the Fairlane and the sporty little Thunderbird. Chrysler's cars had the biggest fins of all, and advertising that called it the forward look. And in September of nineteen fifty-seven, Ford introduced a whole new brand with enormous fanfare. It was called the Edsel.
scenes.caption: THE FORWARD LOOK

scenes.text: The Edsel was one of the most famous failures in American business history. The public found its vertical grille strange, and its price confusing, and the economy was turning down just as it arrived. Within a few years, it was gone. But if your uncle bought one, you probably still tease him about it.
scenes.caption: SEPTEMBER 1957: THE EDSEL

scenes.text: For many young men, the car was also their workshop. On Saturday afternoons, you'd find them in driveways and gas station bays all over America, with the hood up and their heads inside the engine. They traded parts, swapped advice, and argued endlessly about Ford versus Chevy. Some of them have never stopped arguing about it.
scenes.caption: FORD VS CHEVY

scenes.text: Your own first car was probably used. A forty-nine Ford. A fifty-one Chevy with a cracked dashboard. You learned to change the oil yourself, to fix a flat on the side of the road, and to push it down the hill to get it started on a cold morning. And on Friday nights, you washed it, put on a clean shirt, and drove to her house.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST USED CAR

scenes.text: There were no seat belts in most cars, and nobody thought to ask for them. There was no air conditioning, either, so in summer you drove with all the windows down and your elbow resting on the door. And with the new highways being built, you started thinking about how far that car could take you. Chicago. California. Anywhere.
scenes.caption: NO SEAT BELTS, WINDOWS DOWN

scenes.text: Rock and roll was only a couple of years old, and it was still shocking the grown-ups. In nineteen fifty-seven, Elvis had All Shook Up at the top of the charts. Buddy Holly had That'll Be the Day. Jerry Lee Lewis was pounding the piano and setting the whole country on fire.
scenes.caption: 1957: ALL SHOOK UP

scenes.text: And on August fifth, nineteen fifty-seven, a television show from Philadelphia went national. American Bandstand. Every weekday afternoon, a young host named Dick Clark introduced the records, and ordinary teenagers danced in front of the cameras. Kids across the country raced home to watch, and to copy the steps.
scenes.caption: AUGUST 1957: AMERICAN BANDSTAND

scenes.text: On Saturday night, there was the drive-in movie, or the dance hall, or the roller rink. You might see a monster movie, or a western, or a teenage drama that your parents disapproved of. And afterward, a booth at the diner, with a jukebox in the corner, and a plate of fries shared four ways.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY NIGHT

scenes.text: At the movies that year, Elvis starred in Jailhouse Rock, and girls screamed at the screen. And at Christmas, The Bridge on the River Kwai arrived, a war movie your father would go to see twice. Hollywood was fighting hard to pull people away from their televisions, with wide screens, bright color and big stars.
scenes.caption: 1957 AT THE MOVIES

scenes.text: That same year, a young writer named Jack Kerouac published a novel about driving back and forth across America, called On the Road. And on Broadway, a new musical about two rival gangs in New York, called West Side Story, opened in September. The culture was changing, and you could feel it, even in a small town.
scenes.caption: 1957: THE CULTURE WAS CHANGING

scenes.text: For many young people, the newest thing in their hands was a small transistor radio. For the first time, you could carry the music with you. To the beach, to the park, to your bedroom late at night. The radio was no longer the family's. It was yours.
scenes.caption: MUSIC IN YOUR POCKET

scenes.text: The boys wore their hair in crew cuts, or, if they were daring, swept back with grease into a ducktail. They wore white T-shirts and blue jeans rolled at the cuff. The girls wore saddle shoes and full skirts, pearls and cardigans, and their hair in ponytails or short curls. Your parents had opinions about all of it.
scenes.caption: CREW CUTS AND PONYTAILS

scenes.text: If you were eighteen in nineteen fifty-seven, you remember that autumn, even if you don't remember why. Because in just a few weeks, three things happened that changed the country you were stepping into.
scenes.caption: THE AUTUMN OF 1957

scenes.text: In September, in Little Rock, Arkansas, nine Black teenagers tried to enter Central High School. They were your age, or close to it. Crowds screamed at them. The governor sent the National Guard to keep them out. And President Eisenhower sent soldiers of the hundred and first Airborne Division to walk them through the door.
scenes.caption: SEPTEMBER 1957: LITTLE ROCK

scenes.text: You watched it on the evening news. Kids your own age, carrying their schoolbooks, walking past bayonets. Whatever you thought about it then, you never forgot those pictures.
scenes.caption: THE LITTLE ROCK NINE

scenes.text: Then, on October fourth, nineteen fifty-seven, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. It circled the Earth every ninety-six minutes, sending out a little beep that radio operators could hear all over the world. Some people stood in their yards at night trying to spot it.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 4, 1957: SPUTNIK

scenes.text: And here's a strange coincidence. That very same evening, a gentle new family comedy premiered on television. It was called Leave It to Beaver. So on the same night, Americans saw the most comforting picture of family life ever put on a screen, and heard that the Soviets had beaten them into space.
scenes.caption: THE SAME NIGHT: LEAVE IT TO BEAVER

scenes.text: For a young person, it was a confusing message. On one channel, a perfect family in a perfect house. On another, a news anchor talking about Soviet missiles. Many of you remember your parents' faces that week, quieter than usual, and the feeling that the world had suddenly become a little more dangerous.
scenes.caption: A CONFUSING MESSAGE

scenes.text: Overnight, everything changed in the schools. Science and mathematics became a national priority. Within a year, Congress passed a law to pay for science education and student loans. If you were thinking about college, suddenly the government wanted very much for you to go.
scenes.caption: THE SPACE RACE

scenes.text: America tried to answer quickly. On December sixth, nineteen fifty-seven, the Navy's Vanguard rocket rose about four feet off the launch pad, and exploded on live television. The newspapers mocked it. Some called it Flopnik. But less than two months later, on January thirty-first, nineteen fifty-eight, America's first satellite, Explorer One, reached orbit.
scenes.caption: JANUARY 1958: EXPLORER 1

scenes.text: And that same autumn, a new strain of influenza swept the country. People called it the Asian flu. Schools emptied, offices ran short, and according to the C D C, about one hundred sixteen thousand Americans died from it over the next year. Many of you remember being sick in bed for a week, or a classmate who never came back.
scenes.caption: 1957: THE ASIAN FLU

scenes.text: Then, as if all that wasn't enough, the economy slowed down. The recession of nineteen fifty-seven and fifty-eight hit the factory towns hard. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, unemployment climbed above seven percent by the summer of nineteen fifty-eight. Young workers, the last ones hired, were often the first ones let go.
scenes.caption: THE RECESSION OF 1958

scenes.text: So adulthood, for an eighteen-year-old in nineteen fifty-seven, wasn't only freedom. It was responsibility, arriving all at once. A paycheck that had to stretch. A draft card in your wallet. A wedding ring, maybe, and a baby on the way. A world that seemed to change every time you turned on the news.
scenes.caption: RESPONSIBILITY, ALL AT ONCE

scenes.text: A young husband who lost his job at the plant in nineteen fifty-eight didn't have much of a safety net. There was unemployment insurance for a while, and a few odd jobs, and family who helped where they could. Many young couples moved back in with their parents for a few months. Nobody talked about it much, but a lot of people did it.
scenes.caption: MOVING BACK HOME

scenes.text: And yet, ask almost anyone who lived it, and they'll tell you there was something good about it too. You knew your neighbors. Your boss knew your name. A hard-working young person, with a high school diploma, could get a job, buy a car, start a family, and believe that tomorrow would be better than today. For a great many of you, it was.
scenes.caption: TOMORROW WOULD BE BETTER

scenes.text: Adult life also meant belonging. You joined a church, a bowling league, a union local, the Elks, the Rotary, the women's auxiliary. On weeknights there were meetings and suppers and fundraisers. People knew who you were, and they noticed if you didn't show up. It could feel confining. It also meant you were never alone.
scenes.caption: YOU BELONGED

scenes.text: You couldn't vote until you were twenty-one. In nineteen sixty, if you were born in nineteen thirty-nine, you finally could, and your first presidential election was Kennedy against Nixon. Many of you still remember walking into that voting booth for the very first time, and pulling the curtain closed behind you.
scenes.caption: 1960: YOUR FIRST VOTE

scenes.text: If you turned eighteen in nineteen fifty-seven, you're in your late eighties now. You've seen the moon landing, the end of the Cold War, the arrival of the computer and the phone in your pocket. Your grandchildren have grandchildren, some of them. And still, if somebody plays All Shook Up, you know every word.
scenes.caption: LOOKING BACK

scenes.text: You remember the smell of the plant floor, or the clatter of the typing pool. The weight of that first paycheck. The ring in its little velvet box. The sound of Sputnik's beep on the radio. The faces of the classmates you said goodbye to in June of fifty-seven, and the ones you never saw again.
scenes.caption: WHAT YOU REMEMBER

scenes.text: You grew up fast. Faster than young people do today. At eighteen you were working, or serving, or married, or all three. Nobody asked whether you were ready. You just got on with it. And in doing so, your generation built a great deal of the country we live in now.
scenes.caption: YOU GREW UP FAST

scenes.text: So, if you were there, I'd love to hear from you. In the comments, tell me what your first job was, and what it paid. Or tell me where you were the night Sputnik went up. I read every comment, and your stories help shape the next videos on this channel.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR FIRST JOB?

scenes.text: And if you'd like to go back even further, to the kitchen you grew up in, our next story walks through every corner of the American kitchen in nineteen sixty-two. Thank you for spending this time with me. Until next time, take care of yourself.
scenes.caption: NEXT: THE KITCHEN IN 1962
